Hotting up in the Kalahari

By: Laura Byrne | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Climate change is threatening our natural heritage and our very survival

Unique Selling Point:
Climate change - it's a phrase we hear so often, many of us switch off. But the effects of temperature and rainfall changes are not part of the distant future: they're happening right now in our own backyard. Research in one of the most extreme climates on earth, the Kalahari, demonstrates what the future could look like for all of South Africa - and it's putting our rich biodiversity under threat.

Summary:
The Kalahari is named for the Tswana “Kgala” (great thirst) or “Kgalagadi” (waterless place). It spans a vast 900 000km2 semi-desert area of South Africa, Botswana and Namibia. It's one of the most extreme habitats in Southern Africa, with daytime temperatures peaking at over 40 degrees C, and plummeting overnight. Its driest areas receive over 4000 hours of sunshine per year. Kalahari and species are adapted to survive on the edge, so it's here that we'll first see the effects of global climate change on ecosystems and communities.
Worldwide, hundreds of species are already shifting ranges, breeding and feeding patterns in response to warmer temperatures and unpredictable rainfall. A recent UN study reports that 1 million species are under threat: many will be extinct in decades. In 2018, the UN IPCC said there are 12 years left for action if we are to keep global warming to a maximum of 1.5 degrees C above preindustrial levels. Climate change and biodiversity loss pose an existential threat to human beings, increasing poverty, food insecurity, disease, water scarcity and frequency and severity of natural disasters. Poor communities are most at risk, and Africa is particularly vulnerable. South Africa already experiences 2 degrees warming per century, more than twice global average, and growing evidence suggests species are already being affected.
The Kalahari Endangered Ecosystems Project (KEEP) at Tswalu Kalahari Reserve is an ambitious collaboration between 20 biologists undertaking long-term research into the impact of climate change on the whole food system, looking at how changes at grassroots level filter through to the top. It is possibly the first of its kind, and may suggest interventions to help save our wildlife.

Further information:
BIODIVERSITY LOSS
KEEP researchers have already gathered data demonstrating that Kalahari species at all levels of the food chain are struggling to adapt to climate change.

Physiologist Andrea Fuller has been using bio-loggers to track aardvarks at Tswalu for several years. In the first year, 5 out of 6 subjects (as well as at least 6 unlogged aardvark) died of starvation due to drought, which caused a shortage of grass and therefore of the harvester termite, which the aardvark depends on for 81% of its energy needs. Unable to adapt or change their diet, the aardvark simply starved. The trend has continued: usually nocturnal, aardvarks are now frequently found outside their burrows, vulnerable to predators, because they are too hungry to keep themselves warm and must bask in the sun. Many are found emaciated. Andrea predicts that aardvarks will cease to exist in the Kalahari region.

Herpetologist Graham Alexander and his student Tilo are tracking pythons in Tswalu and noticing similar abnormal behaviour. Most of the snakes they pick up are emaciated due to loss of their food source: birds. Some species are continuing their hunting habits into winter when they would usually be less visible, which indicates a shortage of food.

Studies of the meerkats north of Tswalu also show that they are under pressure. Increased heat has led to insufficient food and water, which means the pups are failing to thrive and the meerkats are decreasing in size. There is also a much higher incidence of TB among the meerkats and many other species following drought.

Andrew McKechnie (UP) and Suzie Cunningham (UCT) are running studies of yellow-billed hornbills which suggest that higher temperatures are impacting the breeding success of the species and endangering its survival.

Tswalu guides with years of experience tracking animals in the reserve can speak to the changes in behaviour, ranges and health they observe.

CLIMATE CHANGE, POLICY AND THE HUMAN IMPACT
Although those of us living in bigger cities may have forgotten the recent drought, our farming communities have not. Farmers in the Eastern Cape, Northern Cape and Free State continue to require support from government in the form of fodder and assistance with boreholes and water infrastructure. And this is likely only the beginning of our future with climate change. We will also speak to farmers in the area regarding their experience of the changing climate and how it is challenging their livelihoods and food security for all of us. Local information networks and provincial committees are supposed to provide early warning to farmers, and assist them in dealing with extreme weather such as heat and drought. Are these effective? What else needs to be done?

Increased heat and unstable rainfall means less water and less food. Climate modellers based at Wits can speak to the shifts in temperature and rainfall over time. The Kalahari is increasing in temperature at a rate twice that of the rest of SA: already at the limits of the range at which life can be supported, it is now being pushed over the edge.

Press Release:


Hotting Up in the Kalahari
The effects of climate change are no longer a problem of the future: they’re apparent every day in our changing weather patterns and more frequent extreme weather events. In the Kalahari, an environment of extreme temperatures and scarce rainfall, biodiversity research asks how species will react as temperatures rise at more than double the global average. Dwindling food and water resources push some to the edge of survival and paint a grim picture of Southern Africa’s future with climate change if we don’t take important steps now.
Producer: Laura Byrne | Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


VO1: It’s a summer evening in the Kalahari. The sun is setting and nocturnal species are just beginning to stir.
UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS: Wendy, what’s the plan for tonight?
WENDY PANAINO: So we are currently looking for a pangolin, one of my study subjects, so we can collect some data on her.
DEREK: How do we do that?
WENDY: We use telemetry. That means the animal’s got a tag on her and we’ve got a unit in the car and those two units talk to each other so we can try and pinpoint exactly where she is.
VO2: Wendy Panaino is researching ground pangolins at Tswalu in the Kalahari. Local populations are under pressure from poaching – but an even bigger threat to their survival is looming.
UPSOUND:WENDY: I’ve been focusing on their physiology and their behaviour within the bigger context of climate change. If we want to understand what the long term effects will be on pangolins, we kind of need to know how they’re coping with their current environment
VO3: Dylan Smith heads up research on the reserve.
UPSOUND: DYLAN SMITH: Our three key research themes are impact of climate change, conservation biology and then human impact on the environment.
LINK 1: CLIMATE CHANGE - IT'S A PHRASE WE HEAR SO OFTEN, TRUTHFULLY WE SWITCH OFF. IT’S TOO ABSTRACT, TOO INTANGIBLE…BUT NOT IF YOU CALL THE KALAHARI HOME. HERE, THE EFFECTS ARE ALL TOO CONCRETE.
UPSOUND: FRANCOIS ENGELBRECHT: In the Kalahari we will see many of the fingerprints of climate change occurring first in our region.
VO4: Professor Francois Engelbrecht, a climatologist at the Wits Global Change Institute, says temperatures in southern Africa are increasing at double the global rate.
UPSOUND: FRANCOIS: It's unfortunately quite possible that as soon as the 2040s our region may be three to four degrees warmer.
VO5: Wendy’s research is part of an ambitious study to understand what this means for our wildlife: the Kalahari Endangered Ecosystems Project, or KEEP, founded by physiologist Professor Andrea Fuller and herpetologist Professor Graham Alexander.
UPSOUND: GRAHAM ALEXANDER: What’s really special here is that we’re looking at the ecosystem as a whole and not just single relationships or individual components.
UPSOUND: ANDREA FULLER: We’re looking at how species are responding to climate change. Are they changing their activity? Are they changing their physiology? Can they adapt to change? We can’t go into the future and have a look at how they’re going to respond, but what we can do is look at an analogue of what the future may be like.
UPSOUND: FRANCOIS: Unfortunately our region is also projected to be likely to become generally drier over time. And that includes the more frequent occurrence of multi-year droughts.
VO6: Persistent drought has brought a depletion of the ants and termites on which pangolins rely for food.
LINK 2: PANGOLINS AND TERMITES: IT’S ONE RELATIONSHIP IN A COMPLEX WEB WHICH WE ARE IN DANGER OF LOSING EVEN BEFORE WE HAVE BEGUN TO UNDERSTAND IT.
UPSOUND: DEREK: Early days but are there any signs that the pangolins are under pressure?
WENDY: We’ve only been doing this for four years. and so that’s really just a snapshot in the longer perspective we’re trying to look at. We know if we have a really hot dry season, the following winter seems to put pangolins under pressure.
VO7: Fuller has already seen drought push some animals to the edge of survival. Five years ago, she began a study of the diet and behaviour of Tswalu aardvark, discovering that they rely almost entirely on a single species of termite.
UPSOUND: ANDREA: With too little rainfall there was too little grass, and there were too few harvester termites. We thought and we hoped that the aardvark would simply shift to eating other termites and ant species, but they didn’t. And so unfortunately what we saw is that the animals starved.
VO8: Usually nocturnal, hungry aardvark bask outside their burrows during the day, making them vulnerable to predators. And these researchers have seen a decline in ant and termite populations that could spell big trouble for them and other ant-eaters.
UPSOUND: TILLY MOLETE: If they are specialist feeders, it would be more difficult for them to find their preferred prey.
UPSOUND: VALERY PHAKOAGO: It’s only a few ants and termites available so it worries me that the little that’s left for them, how are they coping with the little prey availability?
UPSOUND: ANDREA: From the data we've obtained so far, we would be very concerned about the future of Aardvark in the Kalahari. My prediction is that we are unlikely to see them there perhaps as soon as 10 years from now.
VO9: As if drought wasn’t enough, intensifying heat itself is a threat to survival.
LINK 3: IT’S JUST AFTER EIGHT IN THE MORNING, ALREADY GETTING HOT. WE’RE HOPING TO MEET SOME CAPE COBRAS AND BOOMSLANG ALSO STARTING THEIR DAY AND TAKING ADVANTAGE OF THE SLIGHTLY COOLER WEATHER. AND THILO IS ON THEIR TRACKS, LITERALLY.
VO10: Thilo Beck is researching snake physiology and behaviour at Tswalu. By implanting a temperature logger, Thilo can observe these snakes remotely.
UPSOUND: THILO: The body temperature of a snake will always align with the temperature of its immediate surrounding. So if the snake is underground, the body temperature will be level with the underground temperature. As soon as the snake goes to the surface […] we see the body temperatures going from 18 degrees to 32.
VO11: His research is showing that climate change could profoundly impact snakes’ behaviour.
UPSOUND: GRAHAM: People normally think of snakes as animals that seek heat – well, in Africa, that’s kind of not really the truth. In fact, in a place like the Kalahari, already snakes have got a big problem with getting too hot most of the time.
UPSOUND: THILO: The snakes are limiting their surface activity to the cooler hours, especially in the summer. So with climate change we might see that these snakes have to shift their activity.
UPSOUND: GRAHAM: And it might actually push them to start becoming nocturnal. We’re often finding anorexic snakes.
UPSOUND: DYLAN: We’re hoping we’ll be able to tweak out what these tolerance levels are for these different species. And that will obviously enable us to take appropriate management measures.
LINK 4: AROUND MIDDAY AND THE HEAT IS TOTALLY DRAINING. ON A DAY LIKE THIS, THE GROUND TEMPERATURES CAN REACH A BAKING 60 DEGREES.
VO12: To keep cool, birds retreat into the shade, or open their beaks to pant. But more time spent dissipating heat means less time spent foraging for food.
UPSOUND: ANDREW MCKECHNIE: That gets translated into a slight loss of body mass per 24 hour cycle. Now that's not necessarily problematic over one day or two days. But if you have ten days in a row of 40 degrees then it becomes a serious problem.
VO13: Professor Andrew McKechnie’s Hot Birds Project has spent a decade studying the effects of increasing temperatures on common Kalahari bird species.
UPSOUND: ANDREW: On very hot days adults struggle to get enough food to the nestlings.
Many nests have been abandoned and the young were often leaving the nest much smaller and weaker than they would under normal conditions. And they typically get eaten by predators within a day or two of leaving the nest.
VO14: The long-term consequences are dire.
UPSOUND: ANDREW: Species that have been common in the Kalahari until now are going to struggle to breed successfully there. And I think by the end of the century, very few of the birds that currently live in the Kalahari are still going to be there.
VO15: And if you think the effects of climate change end with birds and snakes, think again.
UPSOUND: FRANCOIS: It is these droughts that last for three to four years that can bring a farm to its knees, that bring the risk of a day zero event.
VO16: On our current trajectory, says Engelbrecht, we may no longer be able to farm cattle or even maize in southern Africa by the second half of this century.
UPSOUND: FRANCOIS: I can’t sufficiently stress how critical these changes will be for our region. One can indeed say that under a low mitigation climate change future, the southern African region as we know it today will not exist any longer.
LINK 5: IT’S A BLEAK LANDSCAPE AND IT CAN LOOK QUITE EMPTY. BUT LOOK A LITTLE CLOSER AND IT’S ACTUALLY TEEMING WITH LIFE. THE QUESTION IS, FOR HOW LONG?
UPSOUND: ANDREA: Often in nature documentaries you hear about climate change but you still see pristine environments. And what we're seeing is quite the opposite.
UPSOUND: GRAHAM: Systems will become simpler, they’ll become less diverse. Extinction rates will go up.

PROMO 1
VO: The Kalahari: a place of desolate beauty teeming with life. But all this is changing. Climate change is threatening our biodiversity – and we’re losing it faster than we think.

PROMO 2
VO: Climate change: it’s a phrase we hear so often, we switch off. But here in the Kalahari, it’s very real.
UPSOUND: ANDREW: By the end of the century, very few of the birds that currently live in the Kalahari are still going to be there.

PROMO 3
VO: In the Kalahari, researchers are asking how species are responding to climate change. The results are dramatic.
UPSOUND: ANDREA: From the data we've obtained so far, we would be very concerned about the future of Aardvark in the Kalahari.

In the Kalahari, an environment of extreme temperatures and scarce rainfall, biodiversity research asks how species will react as temperatures rise at more than double the global average. Dwindling food and water resources push some to the edge of survival and paint a grim picture of Southern Africa’s future with climate change if we don’t take important steps now. Producer: Laura Byrne | Presenter: Derek Watts Script: VO1: It’s a summer evening in the Kalahari. The sun is setting and nocturnal species are just beginning to stir. UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS: Wendy, what’s the plan for tonight? WENDY PANAINO: So we are currently looking for a pangolin, one of my study subjects, so we can collect some data on her. DEREK: How do we do that? WENDY: We use telemetry. That means the animal’s got a tag on her and we’ve got a unit in the car and those two units talk to each other so we can try and pinpoint exactly where she is. VO2: Wendy Panaino is researching ground pangolins at Tswalu in the Kalahari. Local populations are under pressure from poaching – but an even bigger threat to their survival is looming. UPSOUND:WENDY: I’ve been focusing on their physiology and their behaviour within the bigger context of climate change. If we want to understand what the long term effects will be on pangolins, we kind of need to know how they’re coping with their current environment VO3: Dylan Smith heads up research on the reserve. UPSOUND: DYLAN SMITH: Our three key research themes are impact of climate change, conservation biology and then human impact on the environment. LINK 1: CLIMATE CHANGE - IT'S A PHRASE WE HEAR SO OFTEN, TRUTHFULLY WE SWITCH OFF. IT’S TOO ABSTRACT, TOO INTANGIBLE…BUT NOT IF YOU CALL THE KALAHARI HOME. HERE, THE EFFECTS ARE ALL TOO CONCRETE. UPSOUND: FRANCOIS ENGELBRECHT: In the Kalahari we will see many of the fingerprints of climate change occurring first in our region. VO4: Professor Francois Engelbrecht, a climatologist at the Wits Global Change Institute, says temperatures in southern Africa are increasing at double the global rate. UPSOUND: FRANCOIS: It's unfortunately quite possible that as soon as the 2040s our region may be three to four degrees warmer. VO5: Wendy’s research is part of an ambitious study to understand what this means for our wildlife: the Kalahari Endangered Ecosystems Project, or KEEP, founded by physiologist Professor Andrea Fuller and herpetologist Professor Graham Alexander. UPSOUND: GRAHAM ALEXANDER: What’s really special here is that we’re looking at the ecosystem as a whole and not just single relationships or individual components. UPSOUND: ANDREA FULLER: We’re looking at how species are responding to climate change. Are they changing their activity? Are they changing their physiology? Can they adapt to change? We can’t go into the future and have a look at how they’re going to respond, but what we can do is look at an analogue of what the future may be like. UPSOUND: FRANCOIS: Unfortunately our region is also projected to be likely to become generally drier over time. And that includes the more frequent occurrence of multi-year droughts. VO6: Persistent drought has brought a depletion of the ants and termites on which pangolins rely for food. LINK 2: PANGOLINS AND TERMITES: IT’S ONE RELATIONSHIP IN A COMPLEX WEB WHICH WE ARE IN DANGER OF LOSING EVEN BEFORE WE HAVE BEGUN TO UNDERSTAND IT. UPSOUND: DEREK: Early days but are there any signs that the pangolins are under pressure? WENDY: We’ve only been doing this for four years. and so that’s really just a snapshot in the longer perspective we’re trying to look at. We know if we have a really hot dry season, the following winter seems to put pangolins under pressure. VO7: Fuller has already seen drought push some animals to the edge of survival. Five years ago, she began a study of the diet and behaviour of Tswalu aardvark, discovering that they rely almost entirely on a single species of termite. UPSOUND: ANDREA: With too little rainfall there was too little grass, and there were too few harvester termites. We thought and we hoped that the aardvark would simply shift to eating other termites and ant species, but they didn’t. And so unfortunately what we saw is that the animals starved. VO8: Usually nocturnal, hungry aardvark bask outside their burrows during the day, making them vulnerable to predators. And these researchers have seen a decline in ant and termite populations that could spell big trouble for them and other ant-eaters. UPSOUND: TILLY MOLETE: If they are specialist feeders, it would be more difficult for them to find their preferred prey. UPSOUND: VALERY PHAKOAGO: It’s only a few ants and termites available so it worries me that the little that’s left for them, how are they coping with the little prey availability? UPSOUND: ANDREA: From the data we've obtained so far, we would be very concerned about the future of Aardvark in the Kalahari. My prediction is that we are unlikely to see them there perhaps as soon as 10 years from now. VO9: As if drought wasn’t enough, intensifying heat itself is a threat to survival. LINK 3: IT’S JUST AFTER EIGHT IN THE MORNING, ALREADY GETTING HOT. WE’RE HOPING TO MEET SOME CAPE COBRAS AND BOOMSLANG ALSO STARTING THEIR DAY AND TAKING ADVANTAGE OF THE SLIGHTLY COOLER WEATHER. AND THILO IS ON THEIR TRACKS, LITERALLY. VO10: Thilo Beck is researching snake physiology and behaviour at Tswalu. By implanting a temperature logger, Thilo can observe these snakes remotely. UPSOUND: THILO: The body temperature of a snake will always align with the temperature of its immediate surrounding. So if the snake is underground, the body temperature will be level with the underground temperature. As soon as the snake goes to the surface […] we see the body temperatures going from 18 degrees to 32. VO11: His research is showing that climate change could profoundly impact snakes’ behaviour. UPSOUND: GRAHAM: People normally think of snakes as animals that seek heat – well, in Africa, that’s kind of not really the truth. In fact, in a place like the Kalahari, already snakes have got a big problem with getting too hot most of the time. UPSOUND: THILO: The snakes are limiting their surface activity to the cooler hours, especially in the summer. So with climate change we might see that these snakes have to shift their activity. UPSOUND: GRAHAM: And it might actually push them to start becoming nocturnal. We’re often finding anorexic snakes. UPSOUND: DYLAN: We’re hoping we’ll be able to tweak out what these tolerance levels are for these different species. And that will obviously enable us to take appropriate management measures. LINK 4: AROUND MIDDAY AND THE HEAT IS TOTALLY DRAINING. ON A DAY LIKE THIS, THE GROUND TEMPERATURES CAN REACH A BAKING 60 DEGREES. VO12: To keep cool, birds retreat into the shade, or open their beaks to pant. But more time spent dissipating heat means less time spent foraging for food. UPSOUND: ANDREW MCKECHNIE: That gets translated into a slight loss of body mass per 24 hour cycle. Now that's not necessarily problematic over one day or two days. But if you have ten days in a row of 40 degrees then it becomes a serious problem. VO13: Professor Andrew McKechnie’s Hot Birds Project has spent a decade studying the effects of increasing temperatures on common Kalahari bird species. UPSOUND: ANDREW: On very hot days adults struggle to get enough food to the nestlings. Many nests have been abandoned and the young were often leaving the nest much smaller and weaker than they would under normal conditions. And they typically get eaten by predators within a day or two of leaving the nest. VO14: The long-term consequences are dire. UPSOUND: ANDREW: Species that have been common in the Kalahari until now are going to struggle to breed successfully there. And I think by the end of the century, very few of the birds that currently live in the Kalahari are still going to be there. VO15: And if you think the effects of climate change end with birds and snakes, think again. UPSOUND: FRANCOIS: It is these droughts that last for three to four years that can bring a farm to its knees, that bring the risk of a day zero event. VO16: On our current trajectory, says Engelbrecht, we may no longer be able to farm cattle or even maize in southern Africa by the second half of this century. UPSOUND: FRANCOIS: I can’t sufficiently stress how critical these changes will be for our region. One can indeed say that under a low mitigation climate change future, the southern African region as we know it today will not exist any longer. LINK 5: IT’S A BLEAK LANDSCAPE AND IT CAN LOOK QUITE EMPTY. BUT LOOK A LITTLE CLOSER AND IT’S ACTUALLY TEEMING WITH LIFE. THE QUESTION IS, FOR HOW LONG? UPSOUND: ANDREA: Often in nature documentaries you hear about climate change but you still see pristine environments. And what we're seeing is quite the opposite. UPSOUND: GRAHAM: Systems will become simpler, they’ll become less diverse. Extinction rates will go up. PROMO 1 VO: The Kalahari: a place of desolate beauty teeming with life. But all this is changing. Climate change is threatening our biodiversity – and we’re losing it faster than we think. PROMO 2 VO: Climate change: it’s a phrase we hear so often, we switch off. But here in the Kalahari, it’s very real. UPSOUND: ANDREW: By the end of the century, very few of the birds that currently live in the Kalahari are still going to be there. PROMO 3 VO: In the Kalahari, researchers are asking how species are responding to climate change. The results are dramatic. UPSOUND: ANDREA: From the data we've obtained so far, we would be very concerned about the future of Aardvark in the Kalahari.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Climate change is threatening our natural heritage and our very survival
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Climate change - it's a phrase we hear so often, many of us switch off. But the effects of temperature and rainfall changes are not part of the distant future: they're happening right now in our own backyard. Research in one of the most extreme climates on earth, the Kalahari, demonstrates what the future could look like for all of South Africa - and it's putting our rich biodiversity under threat.
metadata.Summary: The Kalahari is named for the Tswana “Kgala” (great thirst) or “Kgalagadi” (waterless place). It spans a vast 900 000km2 semi-desert area of South Africa, Botswana and Namibia. It's one of the most extreme habitats in Southern Africa, with daytime temperatures peaking at over 40 degrees C, and plummeting overnight. Its driest areas receive over 4000 hours of sunshine per year. Kalahari and species are adapted to survive on the edge, so it's here that we'll first see the effects of global climate change on ecosystems and communities. Worldwide, hundreds of species are already shifting ranges, breeding and feeding patterns in response to warmer temperatures and unpredictable rainfall. A recent UN study reports that 1 million species are under threat: many will be extinct in decades. In 2018, the UN IPCC said there are 12 years left for action if we are to keep global warming to a maximum of 1.5 degrees C above preindustrial levels. Climate change and biodiversity loss pose an existential threat to human beings, increasing poverty, food insecurity, disease, water scarcity and frequency and severity of natural disasters. Poor communities are most at risk, and Africa is particularly vulnerable. South Africa already experiences 2 degrees warming per century, more than twice global average, and growing evidence suggests species are already being affected. The Kalahari Endangered Ecosystems Project (KEEP) at Tswalu Kalahari Reserve is an ambitious collaboration between 20 biologists undertaking long-term research into the impact of climate change on the whole food system, looking at how changes at grassroots level filter through to the top. It is possibly the first of its kind, and may suggest interventions to help save our wildlife.
metadata.Further information: BIODIVERSITY LOSS KEEP researchers have already gathered data demonstrating that Kalahari species at all levels of the food chain are struggling to adapt to climate change. Physiologist Andrea Fuller has been using bio-loggers to track aardvarks at Tswalu for several years. In the first year, 5 out of 6 subjects (as well as at least 6 unlogged aardvark) died of starvation due to drought, which caused a shortage of grass and therefore of the harvester termite, which the aardvark depends on for 81% of its energy needs. Unable to adapt or change their diet, the aardvark simply starved. The trend has continued: usually nocturnal, aardvarks are now frequently found outside their burrows, vulnerable to predators, because they are too hungry to keep themselves warm and must bask in the sun. Many are found emaciated. Andrea predicts that aardvarks will cease to exist in the Kalahari region. Herpetologist Graham Alexander and his student Tilo are tracking pythons in Tswalu and noticing similar abnormal behaviour. Most of the snakes they pick up are emaciated due to loss of their food source: birds. Some species are continuing their hunting habits into winter when they would usually be less visible, which indicates a shortage of food. Studies of the meerkats north of Tswalu also show that they are under pressure. Increased heat has led to insufficient food and water, which means the pups are failing to thrive and the meerkats are decreasing in size. There is also a much higher incidence of TB among the meerkats and many other species following drought. Andrew McKechnie (UP) and Suzie Cunningham (UCT) are running studies of yellow-billed hornbills which suggest that higher temperatures are impacting the breeding success of the species and endangering its survival. Tswalu guides with years of experience tracking animals in the reserve can speak to the changes in behaviour, ranges and health they observe. CLIMATE CHANGE, POLICY AND THE HUMAN IMPACT Although those of us living in bigger cities may have forgotten the recent drought, our farming communities have not. Farmers in the Eastern Cape, Northern Cape and Free State continue to require support from government in the form of fodder and assistance with boreholes and water infrastructure. And this is likely only the beginning of our future with climate change. We will also speak to farmers in the area regarding their experience of the changing climate and how it is challenging their livelihoods and food security for all of us. Local information networks and provincial committees are supposed to provide early warning to farmers, and assist them in dealing with extreme weather such as heat and drought. Are these effective? What else needs to be done? Increased heat and unstable rainfall means less water and less food. Climate modellers based at Wits can speak to the shifts in temperature and rainfall over time. The Kalahari is increasing in temperature at a rate twice that of the rest of SA: already at the limits of the range at which life can be supported, it is now being pushed over the edge.
